claims.text: Rapid thermal shock causes the noble-metal salt precursors to decompose almost simultaneously.
Nearly simultaneous precursor decomposition suddenly produces a high concentration of metal monomers.
The burst of metal monomers produces instantaneous nucleation.
High supersaturation under rapid processing produces ultra-small nuclei.
Near-instantaneous nucleation freezes a homogeneous distribution of metal atoms.
Inhibited atomic mobility prevents elemental segregation.
Suppression of atomic mobility is the key factor governing successful formation of single-phase noble-metal HEA nanoparticles.
Rapid cooling can retain a high-entropy, non-equilibrium state and suppress secondary-phase formation.
Rapid nucleation locks multiple noble metals into a random, single-phase arrangement before significant diffusion occurs.
Slow heating allows differences in precursor reduction kinetics to influence alloy formation.
Slow heating permits greater atomic mobility, thereby promoting phase segregation and elemental clustering.
Relative to slow heating, rapid thermal shock will produce nanoparticles with more uniform elemental mixing and a single-phase alloy structure.
A conventional slow thermal ramp tends to produce phase-separated or elementally segregated noble-metal nanoparticles through sequential precursor decomposition.
The proposed mechanism applies specifically to mixed noble-metal precursors processed under rapid, non-equilibrium conditions.
The mechanism may fail when elemental incompatibilities or equilibrium thermodynamics dominate phase formation.
The heating and cooling rate thresholds required to suppress mobility are unknown and may depend on precursor chemistry and substrate interactions.
The experiment compares otherwise identical precursor mixtures subjected to rapid thermal shock or a slow thermal ramp.
Similar uniform, single-phase products under both rapid and slow processing would falsify the claim that rapid processing is the decisive factor.
